issues.legal_issue: The propounder of a will must establish its execution and testamentary capacity, and must dispel legitimate suspicion arising from the circumstances of execution before the will can be accepted as genuine.
material_facts: The plaintiff relied on a will that left the testator’s property to him and disputed the appellant’s status as the testator’s niece and natural heir.
The will’s genuineness was challenged, and the circumstances surrounding its execution included indications of the testator’s serious illness and other features casting doubt on its execution.
issues.conclusion: The onus of proving a will rests on its propounder. Where suspicious circumstances surround execution, the propounder must explain them to the court’s satisfaction and remove legitimate suspicion before the will can be accepted as genuine.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, the mode of proving a will is generally like that for other documents, subject to the statutory requirements for wills. In the absence of suspicious circumstances, proof of testamentary capacity and the testator’s signature as required by law is sufficient; when suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder’s initial onus becomes heavier and those circumstances must be satisfactorily explained. The Court followed H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Rani Purnima Devi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Dev, and Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur.

predicates.will_proof_case: A party seeks to establish a testamentary document as the deceased person’s will.
predicates.suspicious_execution_circumstances: Circumstances surrounding the document’s execution raise legitimate doubt about whether it was genuinely executed as the deceased person’s will.

issues.definition: When a party seeks to establish a will and suspicious circumstances surround its execution, the propounder must remove legitimate suspicion.

issues.legal_issue: A finding that a will was not proved genuine should not be displaced when the reviewing court fails to give proper weight to the cumulative suspicious circumstances and evidentiary deficiencies identified by the fact-finding court.
material_facts: The testator’s will stated that he had been seriously ill, and he died eight days after the will was made, but satisfactory evidence about the illness and his mental capacity was not produced.
The will incorrectly stated that the testator had no sister and described the sole beneficiary as his real brother, while giving no reason for excluding the natural heir.
A scribe testified that the testator was literate and had written receipts, but the will bore only a thumb impression and no satisfactory explanation was given for not obtaining his signature.
The beneficiary’s son brought the writing book used for the will, the will was made outside the beneficiary’s residence, and the beneficiary gave contradictory accounts of whether he was present.
Only two of the five attesting witnesses were examined; those witnesses sought to deny the testator’s illness and departed from earlier statements made during mutation proceedings.
The first appellate court found the will not proved genuine; the High Court restored the trial court’s finding of due execution without adequately addressing the suspicious circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reversing the first appellate court’s finding that the will was not proved to be genuine. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s judgment and restored the dismissal of the suit based on the will.
issues.legal_principle: Applying the principles under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act and the burden on a propounder to remove legitimate suspicion, the Court held that the cumulative circumstances required satisfactory evidence about the testator’s illness and capacity, an explanation for the thumb impression, and scrutiny of the beneficiary’s role and the witness evidence. The Court followed H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Rani Purnima Devi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Dev, and Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur.

predicates.will_genuineness_dispute: A civil proceeding concerns whether a testamentary document was genuinely executed as a will.
predicates.second_appeal_review: A High Court reviews a first appellate court’s decision in a second appeal.
predicates.appellate_court_found_will_unproved: The first appellate court finds that the propounder has not proved the will genuine.
predicates.high_court_disregarded_cumulative_suspic: The High Court restores a finding that the will was valid without giving sufficient weight to the combined suspicious circumstances identified by the first appellate court.
predicates.serious_illness_near_execution: The testator was described as seriously ill when making the will and died soon afterward, without satisfactory evidence about the illness or the testator’s mental capacity.
predicates.inaccurate_family_recitals: The will contains material inaccuracies about the testator’s family relationships or the beneficiary’s relationship to the testator.
predicates.literate_testator_used_thumbprint: Evidence indicates that the testator was literate, but the will bears a thumb impression rather than a signature and no satisfactory explanation is given.
predicates.beneficiary_involved_in_preparation: The sole beneficiary, or someone closely connected to the beneficiary, played a role in arranging or preparing the will.
predicates.beneficiary_gave_contradictory_accounts: The beneficiary gave conflicting accounts about being present when the will was executed.
predicates.incomplete_attesting_witness_evidence: The propounder examines only some of the attesting witnesses, despite circumstances making further witness evidence relevant.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_departed_from_prior_: Attesting witnesses give evidence inconsistent with their earlier accounts about circumstances surrounding execution of the will.

issues.definition: When a will’s genuineness is disputed in a second appeal, the first appellate court has found it unproved, and the High Court disregards cumulative suspicion supported by one or more of the stated circumstances, the first appellate court’s finding is restored.
